Emergency laparotomy carries a high rate of mortality, especially in those over the age of 70 years, and more needs to be done to improve outcomes, particularly in this group. This could involve increasing acute surgical care manpower, early recognition of patients requiring emergency surgery, development of clear management protocols for such patients, or perhaps even considering centralisation of emergency surgical services to specialist centres with multidisciplinary teams involving emergency surgeons and care of the elderly physicians in hospital and related community outreach services for post-discharge care. Using data on cumulative hospital mortality from 180 days postadmission does not yield a different perspective from using data from 30 days postadmission for the conditions we studied. Day case laparoscopic cholecystectomy is safe, feasible, and cost-effective when patients are carefully selected, providing good patient satisfaction. Regional anesthesia as compared with general anesthesia for surgery in geriatric patients with hip fracture does not decrease morbidity, mortality, or healthcare costs.

Regional anesthesia may be used successfully to treat patients with failed antireflux operations despite its technical difficulty. Effective undergraduate surgical education can be offered in many specialty settings, and removal of the requirement for general surgery in clerkship may lead to a more effective use of all educational opportunities. However, virtual planning and guided surgery for head and neck reconstruction are financially viable even in capped health care systems.

It is essential to address these areas of concern to improve outcomes and quality of life for patients undergoing emergency general surgery laparotomies, particularly those over the age of 70 years.
